query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying ZrB2 with multiple transition metals to form a high‐entropy diboride (e.g., near-equimolar (Zr, Hf, Ti, Nb, Ta)B2) will allow synthesis at lower temperatures (around 1700–1800 °C) while simultaneously enhancing oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance, compared to conventional single-phase ZrB2 produced above 2300 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 synthesized at high temperatures (>2300 °C) with strong Zr–B and B–B interactions but limited oxidation and corrosion resistance under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a high-entropy alloying strategy by incorporating additional transition metals (e.g., Hf, Ti, Nb, Ta) into the ZrB2 matrix to form a single-phase high-entropy diboride.
generation.conditions: Synthesis at reduced temperatures (1700–1800 °C) using methods such as the liquid-phase precursor method; subsequent exposure to high-temperature oxidizing environments and liquid plating-metal baths during service.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanostructured, single-phase high-entropy diboride with a uniform distribution of multiple metal cations that leads to grain refinement and phase stabilization.
generation.mechanism: The increased mixing entropy from the multicomponent alloying decreases the energy barrier for single-phase formation at lower temperatures, retards grain growth, and introduces solid solution strengthening. These features also slow diffusion processes responsible for oxidation and corrosive degradation, hence enhancing high-temperature stability and corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventional single-phase ZrB2 and previous lower-temperature specimens, the high-entropy diboride will exhibit similar or improved mechanical strength and structural integrity while achieving superior oxidation resistance and liquid-metal corrosion durability, all achieved at a lower processing temperature.
generation.baseline: Single-phase ZrB2 prepared at >2300 °C with known issues of high-temperature oxidation and metal corrosion. Prior lower-temperature specimens (prepared at around 1700 °C) did not overcome these durability issues.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to ceramic systems prepared by precursor-based methods at temperatures around 1700–1800 °C and is intended for high-temperature applications (e.g., aerospace, reactor components) where oxidation stability and resistance to liquid metal plating are critical.
generation.uncertainty: While high-entropy diborides have been synthesized at lower temperatures with ultrafine grains and promising structural properties, it remains uncertain if this approach will fully overcome all oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion limitations in service environments; long-term stability and scalability need to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high-entropy diboride samples (e.g., (Zr, Hf, Ti, Nb, Ta)B2) using a liquid-phase precursor method at 1700–1800 °C. Prepare control samples of conventional single-phase ZrB2 produced at >2300 °C and previous lower-temperature specimens. Subject all samples to standardized high-temperature oxidation and liquid metal plating-corrosion tests.
measurements: Determine phase purity and grain size via XRD and electron microscopy.
Measure mechanical properties (hardness, fracture toughness) and densification.
Assess oxidation resistance by thermogravimetric analysis (weight gain/loss) at service-relevant temperatures.
Evaluate structural integrity and corrosion resistance in a controlled liquid-metal plating bath (e.g., molten metal exposure tests, cross-sectional analysis for corrosion depth).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the high-entropy diboride fails to demonstrate statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 20% reduction in oxidation weight gain, maintained or improved mechanical properties, and superior corrosion resistance metrics) compared to both the high-temperature single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.

## Abstract
AbstractA nano-dual-phase powder with ultra-fine grain size was synthesized by the liquid precursor method at 1200 °C. A series of single-phase high-entropy ceramic powders ((Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2) with high purity (C content less than 0.9 wt% and O content less than 0.7 wt%) and ultrafine (average grain sizes of 340–570 nm) were successfully synthesized at 1800 °C. The sample of (TiZrHfNbTa)B2 exhibited a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, and the metal elements were uniformly distributed at the nanoscale, microscale, and macroscale. This method did not apply to the preparation of all high-entropy ceramic powders and was unfavorable for the formation of single-phase high-entropy borides when the size difference factor exceeded 3.9%. The present work provides a guide for the development of ceramic-based composites through precursor impregnation pyrolysis.Keywords: liquid-phase precursor method, high-entropy diboride powders, solid solutions, microstructure, pyrolysis mechanism
